questions.q: In which year did the First World War begin, and which British Viceroy declared India's participation without consulting Indian leaders?
questions.a: The First World War began in 1914; Viceroy Lord Hardinge declared India's entry. A wrong answer (e.g., 1915 or Lord Chelmsford) reveals confusion between the war's outbreak and the 1915 Defence of India Act, or between viceroys — students often conflate Hardinge (1914) with Chelmsford (1916–21) who oversaw the Montagu Declaration.

questions.q: Why did the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League sign the Lucknow Pact in 1916, and what specific concession did the League gain?
questions.a: The Lucknow Pact (1916) reunited Moderates and Extremists in Congress and forged Hindu-Muslim unity; the League secured separate electorates and one-third representation in central legislature. A wrong answer (e.g., "they demanded complete independence" or "Gandhi mediated") shows misunderstanding: the Pact was a constitutional bargain, not a mass movement, and Gandhi was not yet a national leader — students often project later Gandhi-centric narratives onto 1916.

questions.q: A 1917 British report states: "India's contribution in men, money, and material has been magnificent." Using this source, explain how the same contribution became a nationalist argument for self-government.
questions.a: Nationalists argued: 1.3 million Indians served, ₹146 crore in war loans/taxes were extracted, and famines worsened — therefore India had "earned" dominion status. The Montagu Declaration (1917) responded to this moral claim. A wrong answer listing only soldiers or only money misses the triad (men, money, material) and fails to link economic extraction to political demand — a common board-exam omission.

questions.q: Compare the Home Rule Leagues of Tilak (1916) and Besant (1916) in terms of geographical focus, social base, and demand. Why did the British intern Annie Besant in 1917?
questions.a: Tilak's League operated in Maharashtra/Central Provinces with peasant/trader base demanding "Swarajya"; Besant's League worked in Madras/Presidencies with urban intelligentsia demanding "Home Rule" on Irish model. Besant's internment (June 1917) sparked nationwide protests, forcing Montagu's August 1917 declaration. A wrong answer merging the two leagues or missing the Irish parallel shows failure to analyse regional and ideological nuances — a frequent board trap.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The Montagu Declaration (1917) was a genuine British concession to Indian nationalism." Use evidence from the declaration's wording and subsequent 1919 reforms.
questions.a: The Declaration promised "gradual development of self-governing institutions" within the Empire — not independence. The 1919 Government of India Act introduced dyarchy, retaining British control over finance, law, and army. Thus it was a tactical concession to split nationalists, not a genuine transfer of power. A wrong answer calling it "the first step to independence" ignores the deliberate ambiguity of "gradual" and "within the Empire" — a classic board-exam misinterpretation.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (1914–1919) linking five events: War outbreak, Defence of India Act, Lucknow Pact, Home Rule Leagues, Montagu Declaration. Annotate each with one cause and one consequence for Indian nationalism.
questions.a: 1914 War → cause: Viceroy's unilateral declaration → consequence: nationalist resentment. 1915 Defence of India Act → cause: suppress dissent → consequence: radicalised Extremists. 1916 Lucknow Pact → cause: war unity → consequence: Hindu-Muslim constitutional unity. 1916 Home Rule Leagues → cause: Irish model + war-time inflation → consequence: mass political awakening. 1917 Montagu Declaration → cause: Besant internment + war contribution → consequence: raised expectations, later betrayed. A poor timeline lists dates without cause-consequence links — the core board-exam skill.
